result.summary: Chalciope begs Medea to help her sons, and Medea promises. After a sleepless night of fear and shame she nearly poisons herself but is turned by Hera. She meets Jason at Hecate's shrine, gives him the Prometheus charm and tells him how to win the contest.

scenes.title: Chalciope begs Medea's help
scenes.summary: Chalciope makes Medea swear to help save her sons. Medea promises to bring charms to Hecate's temple at dawn.
scenes.stakes: Chalciope's sons face death in the contest; Medea risks betraying her father.

scenes.title: Medea's sleepless night
scenes.summary: Medea agonizes over love, shame and death, and almost takes poison. Hera changes her mind and she waits for dawn.
scenes.stakes: Medea risks disgrace, her family's wrath, or her own life.

scenes.title: Medea drives to Hecate's shrine
scenes.summary: Medea dresses, takes the Prometheus charm and drives to the shrine with her maids. She tells them to keep her secret and stand aloof.
scenes.stakes: Medea risks discovery by her father.

place.name: Aea and the shrine of Hecate

scenes.title: Jason goes to the shrine
scenes.summary: Hera makes Jason splendid. A crow voices her advice and Mopsus sends Jason on alone.
scenes.stakes: Jason needs Medea's help to survive the contest.

scenes.title: Jason and Medea meet
scenes.summary: The two stand speechless, then Jason pleads and cites Ariadne. Medea gives the charm and explains the rites and the stone trick.
scenes.stakes: Jason risks death by bulls and earthborn men; Medea risks her family and homeland.

characters.name: Medea

characters.name: Hecate
characters.description: Goddess of the shrine and of night

characters.name: Prometheus

characters.name: Pasiphae

alias_notes.explanation: Medea invokes Hecate under the title Brimo.
Epithet of the goddess of love, from Cyprus.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable simile of Medea's heart quivering like sunlight reflected from water.
Striking simile of silent lovers like oaks stirred by wind.

analysis.text: Medea's inner conflict between loyalty to family and love for Jason is the emotional centre, driven by divine intervention.
The Prometheus charm and Hecate rites reflect Greek beliefs in magic and night sacrifice.

legacy.text: Apollonius's psychological portrait of Medea in love influenced Virgil's Dido in the Aeneid.

fun_facts.text: Jason's praise of Ariadne's crown of stars recalls the constellation Corona Borealis.

language_notes.text: "Yea" is archaic for "yes" or "indeed"; "haply" means perhaps or by chance.
Chalciope threatens to return from Hades as an avenging Fury, one of the spirits that punished wrongdoers, especially those who broke oaths or harmed kin.
"God help thee" is an exclamation of dismay. Medea asks what healing she could possibly offer against such dreadful curses.
Medea says the oath is to be sworn by Heaven and Earth. "Mother of the gods" refers to Earth.
The mist before her eyes describes dizziness and emotion, a sign of love and joy mixed with confusion.
Hecate was a goddess of witchcraft and night. Medea is her priestess, so charms are brought to her temple.
"Warder" means a guard or watchman; the "wayfarer" is a traveller. Both are named as people who normally stay awake.
"Aeson's son" is Jason. The bulls are the fire-breathing bulls he must yoke to win the Golden Fleece from Medea's father, Aetes.
"The Loves" are several Eros-like spirits who shoot arrows of desire; "nape of the neck" locates where the pain is felt most sharply.
Artemis was believed to bring sudden, painless death to women with her arrows. Medea wishes she had died before Jason arrived.
A Fury was a divine spirit of vengeance and misfortune. Medea blames a god or Fury for bringing Chalciope's sons, who arrived with the Argonauts.
"Glow" here means the blush of modesty. "Scatheless" means unharmed.
"Roof-tree" is the main roof beam, from which she imagines hanging herself.
"Loosening the bands" means untying the cords that fastened the casket.
"The Maiden, the only-begotten" is Hecate, a goddess often called Maiden and only child (of Perses and Asteria in some accounts); the sacrifice must precede use of the charm.
Ichor is the fluid that runs in the veins of gods instead of blood.
Prometheus was chained on Caucasus by Jove for giving fire to humans; an eagle devoured his liver daily.
A cubit is an ancient measure of about the length of a forearm, roughly 18 inches.
Brimo is a title of Hecate as a fearsome underworld goddess.
"Kilted up" means hitched their robes up with a belt so they could run freely.
Leto's daughter is Artemis, goddess of the hunt; Parthenius and Amnisus are rivers associated with her worship in Paphlagonia and Crete.
Medea invents a pretext: she claims fault for having ignored the danger of meeting the strangers, so as to explain why the shrine is empty.
"The bride of Zeus" is Hera, Zeus's wife; she makes Jason unusually beautiful and persuasive in speech.
Cypris is Aphrodite, named for Cyprus; the Loves are her attendant spirits of desire. The crow says Mopsus lacks their favour.
Refers to the prophecy of Phineus, the blind seer who earlier told the Argonauts that Cypris would help them.
Sirius is the Dog Star, whose summer rising was believed to bring disease and drought to flocks.
"Beguile me not with pleasing words" means do not deceive or put me off with flattery. Jason refers to Medea's earlier promise made through her sister.
Ariadne helped Theseus escape the Minotaur's labyrinth in Crete, where her father Minos ruled.
The crown of stars is the constellation Corona Borealis, said to be Ariadne's crown.
"Hive-stored labour of bees" is a periphrasis for honey, used as an offering to Hecate.
"Giants" here means the earthborn armed men who spring from the sown dragon's teeth.

context_notes.text: Medea has been testing Chalciope. Chalciope's sons, fathered by Phrixus, are Medea's nephews, and Jason has promised to yoke Aeetes' fire-breathing bulls.
Argus is Chalciope's eldest son by Phrixus. He has joined Jason's cause and urged his mother to seek Medea's aid.
Chalciope is considerably older than Medea and helped raise her, which is why Medea calls her both sister and mother.
Medea is the daughter of King Aetes of Colchis and a skilled sorceress, so her casket holds real drugs.
Hades is both the god of the dead and the underworld itself, which Greeks imagined as a gloomy place.
Hera favours Jason and the Argonauts, so she shapes Medea's feelings to help them.
Hecate was a goddess of night, magic and crossroads, worshipped at shrines where Medea serves as priestess.
Prometheus, son of the Titan Iapetus, is called Titanian here because the plant grew from his blood.
The stranger is Jason, who must yoke fire-breathing oxen and sow dragon's teeth to win the Fleece from Aeetes.
Mopsus is an Argonaut seer who reads omens from birds. Argus is a son of Phrixus and Medea's nephew, helping the Argonauts.
Crows were considered omen birds, and here Hera speaks through one to guide Jason.
Medea is a priestess of Hecate, goddess of night and witchcraft. The rites she describes are her own, performed at night with a pit sacrifice.
Jason must face fire-breathing bulls and armed men grown from sown teeth. These are the tasks Aeetes sets for the Golden Fleece.

literary_notes.text: Chalciope's threat to return as an avenging Fury is an extreme appeal, intended to bind Medea through fear and guilt.
Medea's blush and joy reveal her hidden love for Jason, even as she speaks of family duty.
Medea's renewed shame and fear suggest the inner conflict and betrayal of her father that will follow.
The hush falling over sailors, travellers, a grieving mother and even the dogs makes Medea's wakefulness in the next sentence stand out sharply.
Her fluttering heart is likened to a reflected sunbeam trembling on a wall, conveying restless, unstable agitation.
The Loves are shown as archers aiming arrows at the heart, making love an external attack she suffers.
Her imagined mocking of the Colchian women shows how much she fears shame, using their voices to dramatise her inner conflict.
The sweetness of the sun and her playmates shows why life draws her back from death, a turn of feeling before Hera's influence is named.
Medea's forgetfulness of present and coming woes hints at the suffering her love for Jason will bring.
The earth bellows and Prometheus groans at the cutting of the root, making the plant seem alive and suffering.
Medea is compared to Artemis with her nymphs and cowering beasts, elevating her to divine majesty and showing awe in the people.
The maids approve a crafty plan built on a lie, though Medea has hidden her true feelings for Jason.
Mopsus rejoices because he already foresees how things will end, hinting at success tied to Medea.
Jason is compared to Sirius: beautiful to see yet bringing harm, foreshadowing the pain his beauty will cause Medea.
The silent lovers are likened to still trees that murmur once the wind stirs, just as Love will soon set them talking.
Medea's melting heart is compared to dew warmed by morning light on roses, showing her softening gently under love.
